events.description: When her father's Plymouth lands were divided into four purparts, the two believed to hold the coal beds were drawn by Elizabeth (Harvey) Pringle and Sarah (Harvey) Lane; Thomas Pringle mined coal there with brothers-in-law Jameson Harvey and George Lane in the 1830s. [R4-S1]

bio:
Elizabeth Harvey was born in Plymouth Township, Luzerne Co., PA, on 20 September 1790, a daughter of Elisha Harvey, born at North Lyme, Connecticut, in 1758, and Rosanna Jameson, born in 1758, a daughter of Robert and Agnes (Dixon) Jameson of Hanover Twp., formerly of Voluntown, Connecticut. Her parents had married in 1786. After her father's death in 1800 her mother kept the stone farmhouse in Plymouth, and it was there, on 5 September 1813, that Elizabeth married Thomas Pringle, eldest son of Samuel and Martha (Lamoreux) Pringle, with her brother-in-law the Rev. George Lane officiating. When the Harvey lands were divided she drew one of the two lots believed to hold coal, and in the 1830s her husband worked a mine there with her brother Jameson Harvey and George Lane.

In 1836–37 the family sold up and moved to Kingston, to the old Peter Sharp house at the end of the lane that became Pringle Street. Thomas died there in 1861, and Elizabeth died at Kingston on 26 May 1868. Their children included Sarah, born in 1814, who married Elias Culver; Rosanna Harvey (1816–1875); the twins Martha, who died in infancy, and Samuel, born in 1818; Millicent (1820–1865); the twins George Lane (1822–1886), who was killed by lightning, and Caroline, born in 1822; and Alexander Jameson (1824–1881). She also raised an orphaned great-niece, a granddaughter of her brother Silas.
sources: [R4-S1] Oscar Jewell Harvey, The Harvey Book (1899), entry (189) Elizabeth Harvey, pp.134-138; entry (180) Elisha Harvey; division of Elisha Harvey lands (pp.694-695 area) (secondary) https://archive.org/details/harveybookgiving00harv

summary: Daughter of Elisha Harvey of Plymouth (1790–1868) and wife of Thomas Pringle, whose coal land the family worked before moving to Kingston in 1837.
